title: The Price of a Pretty Face: Does Attractiveness Pay When Controlling for Intelligence?
text:
Does society financially reward physical appearance alongside cognitive test scores? In labor economics, the hypothesis that more attractive or taller workers earn higher salaries is known as the beauty premium. For STAT 386 students learning data acquisition and statistical modeling, testing this hypothesis is a practical exercise in estimating conditional associations while accounting for correlated traits and observational limitations. For instance, Body Mass Index (BMI) alone cannot distinguish muscle mass from fat, so pairing BMI with waist circumference helps separate overall mass from body composition, while adjusting for sex and adolescent IQ reduces demographic confounding.






NoteMotivating Question



How are physical attractiveness (looks), height (height), standardized BMI (bmi), waist circumference (waist), sex (sex), and adolescent cognitive ability (iq) conditionally associated with an individual’s logged annual salary (log(income)) in the 1993 survey wave when holding the other observed variables constant?

title: The Price of a Pretty Face: Does Attractiveness Pay When Controlling for Intelligence?
section: 2. Data Source, Survey Wave & Variable Documentation
text:
2. Data Source, Survey Wave & Variable Documentation
The data comes from the Wisconsin Longitudinal Study (WLS) Version 2026_v1 (Herd, Carr, & Roan, 2014), which tracks over 10,000 Wisconsin high school graduates from the class of 1957 across multiple decades. The earnings and physical body measurements analyzed in this post come from the 1993 survey year—collected 36 years after 1957, when the surveyed graduates were around 54 years of age (the target age reflected in the interactive prediction module below). In the prediction module, a 4.1423 (414.23%) inflation factor is applied to convert 1993 dollar purchasing power into 2026 USD purchasing power.

Variable Dictionary & Measurement Definitions
To clarify how each trait is operationalized in the 1993 WLS wave (among complete cases with annual earnings above $1,000), Table 1 documents all seven variables used in the regression analysis:









Variable
WLS Column Code
Scale / Units
Detailed Description & Wave Context




income
r04_z_p001re_i
1993 USD (> $1,000)
Annual wages and salary earned by the respondent in the 1993 survey wave (at roughly 54 years of age). Filtered to positive earners with income > $1,000 and transformed via natural logarithm (log(income)) for linear modeling. Multiplied by the 4.1423 inflation factor in the interactive calculator to express 1993 USD in 2026 USD purchasing power.


looks
r06_z_a103rea_i
1–10 rating scale
An arbitrary rating of the attractiveness of the observational unit’s 1957 high school yearbook photo from 1 to 10. The exact year of evaluation is unknown, though ratings are assumed to have been completed all at once by a trained rating panel.


bmi
ad_g_srbmi
Standardized SD units ($ ext{kg/m}^2\() | Standardized Body Mass Index originally measured in **\) ext{kg/m}^2$** (centered at a reference BMI of \(22  ext{ kg/m}^2\)), with a standard deviation of around \(2.54 ext{ kg/m}^2\) given the 1993 survey wave (filtered to bmi > -4 to remove negative missingness codes).



height
r06_z_x010rec_q
Inches (in)
Self-reported standing height of the respondent measured in inches during the 1993 survey wave (filtered to valid measurements height >= 0).


waist
r06_z_x457re_i
Inches (in)
Self-measured waist circumference in inches collected in the 1993 wave (filtered to waist > 0), included alongside standardized BMI to help distinguish central adiposity from overall body mass.


iq
ad_g_gwiiq_j
IQ points
Adolescent cognitive score derived from high school administration of the Henmon-Nelson Test of Mental Ability, scaled in standard IQ points (filtered to iq >= 0).


sex
sd_z_sexrsp
Binary (0 = Male, 1 = Female)
Biological sex of the respondent, originally coded in WLS as 1 = Male and 2 = Female, recoded via sex - 1 so that 0 = Male is the baseline reference category and 1 = Female.





Ethical Considerations
Even when working with a public research archive rather than scraping a live website, responsible data acquisition requires strict ethical compliance:

Local Processing Only: WLS terms of use explicitly prohibit uploading raw participant records to external AI platforms (such as ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini) to protect participant confidentiality and prevent unauthorized data retention.
Anonymity & Generalizability: Researchers must never attempt to de-anonymize graduates. Furthermore, because the sample reflects a 1957 Midwestern cohort observed in 1993 around age 54 and relies on subjective panel ratings of static yearbook photos, results carry historical and measurement caveats.

title: The Price of a Pretty Face: Does Attractiveness Pay When Controlling for Intelligence?
section: 3. How to Get Started with Massive Survey Archives
text:
3. How to Get Started with Massive Survey Archives
Longitudinal research repositories like WLS are a great place to start building a dataset without intensive web scraping. The main challenge is scale: the raw WLS download is a 425 MB Stata (.dta) file with roughly 12,500 columns.
To get started on your own machine without crashing R, use the labelled::lookfor() function to search column descriptions by keyword, then pipe haven::read_dta() into dplyr::select() and filter() to strip negative missingness codes and recode binary indicators:


Code
library(haven)
library(dplyr)
library(labelled)

# Search the 12,500 variables by keyword before subsetting
my_data <- read_dta("wls_main_public_2026_v1.dta")
lookfor(my_data, "income")

# Select target variables, filter invalid/missing codes, and recode sex (0 = Male, 1 = Female)
my_subset <- my_data |>
  select(
    height = r06_z_x010rec_q,
    looks  = r06_z_a103rea_i,
    iq     = ad_g_gwiiq_j,
    income = r04_z_p001re_i,
    sex    = sd_z_sexrsp,
    bmi    = ad_g_srbmi,
    waist  = r06_z_x457re_i
  ) |>
  filter(height >= 0, looks >= 0, iq >= 0, income > 1000, waist > 0, bmi > -4) |>
  na.omit()

my_subset$sex <- my_subset$sex - 1

title: The Price of a Pretty Face: Does Attractiveness Pay When Controlling for Intelligence?
text:
4. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) & Model Findings
After cleaning and filtering out non-positive or sub-$1,000 incomes (income > 1000), the final complete-case dataset contains N = 2,990 participant observations across 7 variables (6 predictors and 1 response). Figure 1 displays the initial faceted scatterplots of 1993 annual income against each predictor alongside the correlation heatmap.

  
    
    Figure 1A: Raw 1993 annual income compared with each predictor in the complete-case sample (N = 2,990).
  
  
    
    Figure 1B: Correlation heatmap showing a strong r = -0.76 correlation between height and sex.
  

Two patterns immediately stand out. First, raw annual income in 1993 is heavily right-skewed with extreme high earners ($300,000), making a logarithmic transformation (log(income)) essential for linear modeling. Second, height and sex are strongly correlated (r = -0.76), while looks and waist correlate negatively (r = -0.27).

Baseline Log-Linear Model & Tightened Interpretation
Fitting the baseline OLS regression on log-transformed 1993 income (lm(log(income) ~ height + looks + iq + bmi + waist + sex)) explains 31.55% of the variance in log-earnings ($ ext{Adjusted } R^2 = 0.3141$, \(F = 229.1\), \(p < 2.2     imes 10^{-16}\), residual standard error \(\hat{\sigma} pprox 0.71\) log-points):

Holding IQ, height, sex, standardized BMI, and waist circumference constant, the regression table supports the reported conditional associations: each 1-unit increase in looks is conditionally associated with a 4.32% increase in predicted geometric mean annual income (95% CI: +2.76% to +5.91%, \(p = 4.46  imes 10^{-8}\)). Adolescent IQ shows a strong positive conditional association (+1.22% per IQ point, \(t = 13.27\)), and height shows a modest +1.03% association per inch once sex is controlled.
Conditional Associations vs. Causality: Care is required not to over-interpret these slopes. The estimated coefficients describe conditional associations within the analytic sample rather than causal evidence that physical attractiveness or IQ directly causes higher pay. Unobserved or omitted variables—including educational attainment, occupation, industry, hours worked, and non-random selection into the complete-case, income-over-$1,000 sample—may still confound or mediate these relationships. Furthermore, while the diagnostic plots and Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) check (Figure 2) show that even the highest VIFs (height ≈ 2.40, sex ≈ 2.38) sit well below the threshold of 5, low VIFs address collinearity only; they do not establish causality or validate all regression assumptions (such as zero conditional mean error, homoscedasticity, or absence of measurement error).

  
    
    Figure 2A: Diagnostic plots for the log(income) model show centered residuals and low leverage.
  
  
    
    Figure 2B: All predictor VIF scores remain below 5, addressing collinearity among included predictors only.
  



Exploring Interactions: IQ, Sex, BMI, and Waist
Next, I visually tested whether trait slopes vary by sex or body shape (Figure 3). While the slopes for waist and BMI across sex (Figure 3B) and BMI across waist tertiles (Figure 3C) are nearly flat and parallel, plotting raw 1993 dollar income against IQ by sex (Figure 3A) shows a much steeper dollar slope for men than for women.

  
  Figure 3A: In raw 1993 dollars, the conditional slope on IQ appears steeper for men (blue) than for women (orange).



  
    
    Figure 3B: Waist and BMI slopes across sex are nearly flat and parallel.
  
  
    
    Figure 3C: Grouping waist size into tertiles shows minimal BMI × waist interaction.
  

When adding the sex * iq interaction term to the log-income model (model2 <- lm(log(income) ~ height + looks + bmi + waist + sex + iq + iq*sex)), the estimated interaction coefficient is -0.00142 (p = 0.432). Why does the steep raw-dollar gap shrink on the log scale? Because an approximately similar percentage return per IQ point naturally translates into a larger raw-dollar gap for the group with the higher baseline wage. However, the reported IQ-by-sex p-value of 0.432 does not establish identical returns between men and women—failing to reject a null interaction is not proof that the true interaction is zero. Reporting a 95% confidence interval for the interaction slope (approximately [-0.0050, +0.0021] log-income points per IQ point, or -0.50% to +0.21% per IQ point) better communicates the estimation uncertainty: the data are compatible with anything from a modest female penalty to a slight female advantage in percentage returns to IQ.

5. Cohort-Specific Model Illustration (1993 Wave, Age ~54)
The interactive calculator below is a cohort-specific model illustration based on the 1957 Wisconsin high school cohort surveyed in 1993 at roughly 54 years of age. All dollar outputs apply a 4.1423 (414.23%) inflation factor to convert 1993 USD purchasing power into 2026 USD purchasing power. Honestly it’s just put in here for fun, and predicts your salary based on the coefficients garnered, at the age of 54.






CautionDistinguishing exp(predicted log income) from Mean Expected Dollar Income



Because the OLS model is fit on log(income), simply exponentiating the linear predictor—\(\exp(x'\hat{ eta})\)—estimates the conditional median / geometric mean dollar income, not the conditional mean (expected) dollar income \(E[ ext{income} \mid X]\). title: The Price of a Pretty Face: Does Attractiveness Pay When Controlling for Intelligence?
section: 6. Limitations of the Prediction Module & Complete-Case Selection
text:
6. Limitations of the Prediction Module & Complete-Case Selection
To interpret both the regression table and the interactive prediction module responsibly, several methodological and sample-selection limitations must be emphasized:

Complete-Case & income > $1,000 Sample Selection: Filtering the original ~10,317 WLS cohort down to N = 2,990 complete observations with income > $1,000 removes over 70% of the cohort—excluding individuals who were out of the labor force in 1993 (such as homemakers, early retirees, or disabled respondents), workers earning $1,000 or less, and participants who did not return the 1993 mail/phone anthropometry questionnaire or lacked rated yearbook photos. Because labor force participation at age 54 in 1993 varied systematically by sex, health, and family structure, conditioning on positive earnings and complete data can introduce sample selection bias (e.g., Heckman-type selection).
Omitted Variables & Non-Causal Conditional Associations: The baseline specification omits critical human-capital and labor-supply variables—most notably educational attainment, occupation, industry, annual hours worked, and full-time vs. part-time status. Consequently, the large negative coefficient on sex (-0.8366 log-points) and the positive coefficients on looks and iq reflect unadjusted differences in hours worked and occupational sorting as well as direct wage differences. While the regression table supports the reported conditional associations, low VIFs (< 2.5) address collinearity among the six included predictors only; they do not establish causality or validate all regression assumptions.
Retransformation Bias & Wide Individual Prediction Uncertainty: In a log-linear model, \(\exp(x'\hat{ eta})\) estimates the conditional median/geometric mean rather than the conditional arithmetic mean expected dollar income, which requires a retransformation adjustment. Moreover, with \(R^2 = 0.3155\) (\(\hat{\sigma} pprox 0.71\)), nearly 68.5% of the variance in logged 1993 earnings remains unexplained, resulting in a 95% individual prediction interval that spans roughly fourfold below to fourfold above the point estimate.
Historical Cohort Specificity & Proxy Measurement Error: The model is calibrated on 1957 Wisconsin high school graduates observed in 1993 at approximately age 54. Labor market returns, gender norms, and demographic diversity in the modern U.S. economy differ markedly from mid-century Wisconsin. Additionally, looks is based on a single 1957 high school yearbook photograph (rated at an unknown date) and bmi/waist are self-reported in 1993, introducing measurement error and temporal mismatch.

title: Introduction: Purpose of the Blog Post and Exigence for the Student
text:
Congratulations! You’ve landed your first internship or job working with data analysis! As a fellow student and aspiring data scientist, here are some principles, practices, and tools I’ve found helpful in my collaboration with professionals in other fields.





Curiosity > conclusiveness
Communicate frequently and extensively
Foster mutual understanding

To be curious is better than to be conclusive. Curiosity allows for dialogue and sharing of information, which promotes trust and openness.
Frequent and extensive communication can improve workflow, streamline decision-making, and reduce points of friction. In separate work as a freelance graphic designer, I encountered this frequently with the ‘completion’ of a product only to recognize that I had failed to involve the client throughout the process. Communication throughout a project decreases the likelihood of drastic revisions later down the road.
Fostering mutual understanding can come in many forms. It often looks different as a project moves through different phases. This may look like sharing of jargon, establishing ways to keep contact, setting expectations for turnaround and response times, or a multitude of other helpful practices. The core philosophy at work is a preference for effort over the assumption of connection.




Statistics are a powerful form of evidence, crucial to a multitude of fields, which include: politics, sports, engineering, aeronautics, the pharmaceutical industry, and the wider scope of healthcare.
Rhetors in all ages have used statistics to support all sorts of causes. The newspaper industry often uses statistics directly following bold headlines to qualify those bold headlines. Consider the following:

The hidden divide that makes life less affordable for some Americans New data shows that record-high monthly payments for car loans and student loans are adding huge costs to some budgets. (The Washington Post)
U.S. Budget Deficit Nears $2 Trillion, a Reality Check for Trump’s Cost Cutting Higher interest rates are inflating borrowing costs as the Trump administration spends on the Iran war and tariff refunds. (The New York Times)
Egg prices have quadrupled, chicken has doubled: the cost of US inflation in 10 items Egg prices are up 310% since 2005. But it’s not the only staple with soaring prices. (The Guardian)

Salesmen and saleswomen may use statistics to inspire potential buyers. Consider the following common phrases:

“Join 3 million other subscribers!”
“Recommended by 9 out of 10 dentists!”
“Kills 99.9% of bacteria!”

In small and big ways, statistics can be used to powerful effect. Mark Twain remarked on this when he wrote in his autobiography, “There are three kinds of lies: lies, damned lies, and statistics.”
Equipped with a plethora of models and algorithms, you have the ability to heavily influence perceptions surrounding any topic. As Uncle Ben said to Peter Parker: “With great power comes great responsibility.”
Unlike doctors, who take upon them the Hippocratic Oath, statisticians do not formally uphold any commitment. With that in mind, I invite you to commit yourself to a pursuit of truth.




Collaboration tools: These tools allow you to share images, PDFs, and other documents with your fellow professionals. Many professionals within the STEM fields are familiar with GitHub, but outside of GitHub, many more are familiar with Google Drive.

Examples: GitHub, Google Drive, Box, Dropbox

Visualization tools: A picture is worth a thousand words, the saying often goes. I might say: a good graphic is worth a lot of data points. Charts, pictures, and graphs are a powerful way to display findings and communicate conclusions. Outside of the field of statisticians, many are familiar with bar charts, histograms, and density maps.

Examples: Quarto, Jupyter Notebook

Data cleaning tools: These are the unsung heroes of data analytics. Almost all data that you will work with will require some level of cleaning or pruning to be usable.

R packages: tidyverse, stringr, lubridate
Python packages: pandas, pyjanitor, TheFuzz















Acronym
Test Name
Score Type (Numeric or Categorical)




OPI
Oral Proficiency Interview
Categorical (Proficiency ratings such as Novice, Intermediate, Advanced, Superior)


TOCFL
Test of Chinese as a Foreign Language
Both (Numeric scaled scores and Categorical bands/levels 1-6)


TOPIK
Test of Proficiency in Korean
Both (Numeric total scores and Categorical levels 1-6)


JCAT
Japanese Computerized Adaptive Test
Numeric (Total score from 0 to 400)


JLPT
Japanese-Language Proficiency Test
Both (Numeric scaled scores and Categorical levels N5-N1)



While analyzing national language test scores, I was given a survey containing around hundreds of student responses on their background as language learners. Generally, this was collected using short responses. Everything from student names to their courses was entered manually in free response. While the open environment was helpful for students to freely write about their background and provide context for the answers they provided, it also provided a challenge for data analytics.
One such question posed to the students was “How long have you been learning this language?” This was followed by a self-evaluation of their experience. Some students counted in the time they had been actively learning the language, if native speakers, from birth. Some students answered in years and others in months or weeks. Yet others used decimals and rudimentary mixed fractions and numbers to communicate their experience.
All of these responses needed to be cleaned to group the students by specific language learned (which was also self-entered!). Using string matching for specific phrases, I worked through the most frequent ‘outliers’, as we had determined to use a unit of months for the final dataset. When run in order, the sequential code blocks would first catch the responses with portions such as ‘years’, ‘weeks’, or ‘months’, and add a string which would resist further manipulation based on following grepl conditions.
All of this follows rudimentary statistical procedures. Take a look at your data, make a plan to clean it, implement the plan, save periodically and frequently, and preserve the initial dataset to avoid overwriting important information.
Beyond the codeblocks, there was also frequent communication with Dr. Moody. When I came to blocks such as conflicting responses from the same student or questions about hyperparameters for Bayesian models, I turned to the in-field experts. I could make guesses based on the test score data I had received, but I also trusted and knew I could pull on the expertise of the professors within their respective language departments. Each professor that was a part of this project had years of teaching experience and a familiarity with student performance on these tests that I simply did not have, one that was specific to the language learners at Brigham Young University.




In this experience, I have learned that applying these general principles of good communication and these specific guidelines for cross-discipline collaboration is worth it.
So as you start your new position as an intern or data scientist, try applying the following!

Curiosity > conclusiveness.
Communicate frequently and extensively.
Foster mutual understanding.
Pursue truth!






Chalabi, M. (2025, March 22). Egg prices have quadrupled, chicken has doubled: The cost of US inflation in 10 items. The Guardian.
Rappeport, A. (2026, October 16). U.S. budget deficit nears $2 trillion, a reality check for Trump’s cost cutting. The New York Times.
Twain, M. (1906, September 7). Chapters from my autobiography. North American Review. Project Gutenberg.
Weil, J. Z. (2026, October 15). The hidden divide that makes life less affordable for some Americans. The Washington Post.

Communicate frequently and extensively.
Foster mutual understanding.
Pursue truth!
